passage:
Placement cell note, Thursday. Vishal came for a mock interview. On the panel's questions Vishal answered in clear, polished English, calm and confident. Good. Afterwards I walked out to the car park and saw Vishal speaking to the college driver, Bhola Ram. The tone changed at once: Hindi in the driver's local dialect, quick and easy, a laugh, a hand on the shoulder.
Then a second scene: when two juniors approached, Vishal answered them in fast English and turned away, and the juniors' faces fell. I asked Vishal to talk with me afterwards. We talked about how language can bring people in or keep them out. Vishal said, "I didn't notice." Next day I saw Vishal greet the juniors in Hindi first.
Trisha, placement officer

qa.q: Who was the college driver that Vishal spoke to in the car park?
qa.a: The college driver was Bhola Ram.

qa.q: What might Vishal have been feeling when saying "I didn't notice"?
qa.a: Vishal was probably surprised and a little embarrassed. The words suggest the switch had happened without thought, and Vishal had not meant to leave the juniors out.

qa.q: What did Trisha do after seeing the switch, and what changed the next day?
qa.a: Trisha talked with Vishal about how language can include or exclude. The next day Vishal greeted the juniors in Hindi first.

qa.q: How might the juniors have felt when Vishal answered them in fast English and turned away?
qa.a: The juniors probably felt dismissed or small, since their faces fell. A friendly switch to Hindi the next day would tell them they were welcome.

grounding: A young adult moves into polished English for an interview and into a local tongue with the driver, and learns that language can include or exclude.

passage:
Saturday night. Interview went okay, I think. I spoke English the whole time, and used long words, and I felt very grown-up.
But something bothered me. This morning, before my cousins arrived, I chatted to Lakshmi akka in Tamil in the kitchen, and we laughed about the burnt dosa. Then my cousins came in, and I heard myself say to her in English, "Could you please bring the tea?" in that stiff voice, and Lakshmi akka looked at me strangely and said nothing.
I don't know why I did it. I think I wanted my cousins to see me as someone who employs people, not someone who jokes with them. That is an awful reason.
I'll say sorry tomorrow, in Tamil.
— Vandana

qa.q: What did Vandana say to Lakshmi akka in English when the cousins came in?
qa.a: Vandana said, "Could you please bring the tea?" in a stiff voice.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel after looking back on the morning?
qa.a: Vandana felt uneasy and ashamed. Calling the English request "an awful reason" shows a guilty conscience about signalling status.

qa.q: What did Vandana decide to do about it, and why is that a good step?
qa.a: Vandana plans to say sorry the next day in Tamil, the language they share warmly. That repairs the hurt and shows respect.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi akka have felt when the tone changed to stiff English?
qa.a: Lakshmi akka may have felt hurt or shut out, since the warm chatting turned into a formal order. Looking strangely and saying nothing suggests the change was felt.

grounding: A young adult uses polished English at an interview and local tongue at home, and notices using language to signal status with someone hurts.

passage:
Home from college in Bengaluru for the summer, Anjali walked with her cousin Binita to the hardware shop in their small town in Bihar. The shop was crowded. Anjali heard herself say, in crisp English, "Excuse me, I need a three-pin plug, and could you please be quick?"
The shopkeeper, who had known her since she was six, blinked. He answered slowly in Maithili, then served her first, ahead of an older farmer.
Outside, Binita said quietly, "You never talk to Ramesh chacha like that."
Anjali's face grew warm. She had wanted the plug quickly, yes, but she had also wanted to sound like someone important. And the old farmer had been pushed back because of it.
The next day she went back for a bulb. In Maithili she asked after Ramesh chacha's granddaughter's exams, and waited her turn.

qa.q: What did Anjali ask for at the hardware shop?
qa.a: Anjali asked for a three-pin plug.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when Binita spoke to her outside?
qa.a: Anjali felt embarrassed and ashamed, her face growing warm as she saw she had used English to sound important and pushed the farmer back.

qa.q: What small change did Anjali make, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She went back and spoke in Maithili, asked about the family and waited her turn, which undid the status signal and treated everyone equally.

qa.q: How did the farmer likely feel when Anjali was served first?
qa.a: The farmer probably felt overlooked and small, pushed back in the queue because Anjali's English signalled status.

grounding: A young adult uses polished English with a local shopkeeper to signal status, then becomes aware of it and switches back.

passage:
Tariq had spent the morning at an internship interview in central London, speaking in the polished, careful English his university had taught him. He'd done well. On the ride home, he was still in that voice.
The driver, Abebe, asked in friendly, accented English whether he'd had a good day. Tariq answered in short, clipped sentences, the way the interview panel had spoken to him: correct, cool, a little distant.
Abebe went quiet and turned up the radio.
Tariq noticed. It was the same quiet his grandmother went into when his cousins spoke fast English around her at Eid, and she couldn't follow. He'd always hated that.
He leaned forward. "Sorry, long day. Yes, it went well, I think. Where are you from?"
"Ethiopia. Addis."
"My grandmother's from Lahore. She says London is too fast."
Abebe laughed and turned the radio down. They talked about grandmothers until the car stopped.

qa.q: Where had Tariq spent the morning?
qa.a: Tariq had spent the morning at an internship interview in central London.

qa.q: What made Tariq change his tone with Abebe?
qa.a: Tariq felt uneasy and a little ashamed when Abebe went quiet, because it reminded him of his grandmother's hurt quiet when cousins spoke fast English around her.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Tariq's clipped, cool voice sounded distant and superior; apologising, softening his tone and asking a warm question put them on equal terms.

qa.q: How did Abebe likely feel during the clipped answers?
qa.a: Abebe likely felt dismissed and shut out, which is why Abebe went quiet and turned up the radio.

grounding: A young adult carries polished interview English into a talk with a driver and signals status, then notices and softens.

passage:
On the medical ward in Chennai, Vidya, a final-year student, spoke English to the consultants on rounds and Tamil to the patients' families. But with Lavanya, the ward attendant who had worked there twenty years, Vidya had slipped into rapid English, full of terms: "Please prep bed six for the NG tube, and do the I/O charting."
Lavanya nodded, then quietly asked another attendant what "I/O" meant.
Vidya saw it from the nursing station. Her stomach dropped. She hadn't meant to sound superior, but she had been enjoying sounding like a doctor.
After rounds she went over. "Akka, I spoke too fast earlier. I meant, keep a note of how much water he drinks and how much urine comes, for bed six. In Tamil, I should have said it."
Lavanya smiled. "Twenty years I've done that chart, ma. I just didn't know the English name."
Vidya laughed and asked her to teach her the ward's shortcuts.

qa.q: Who did Vidya speak Tamil with?
qa.a: Vidya spoke Tamil to the patients' families.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when she saw Lavanya ask another attendant?
qa.a: Vidya felt a drop in her stomach, embarrassed and uneasy that her rapid English had made Lavanya feel left out.

qa.q: What small, kind step did Vidya take?
qa.a: She went back, apologised for speaking too fast, explained the task in plain words and asked Lavanya to teach her the ward's shortcuts.

qa.q: How did Lavanya see the situation?
qa.a: Lavanya felt a little left out by the English term but not small, since she had done that chart for twenty years and simply didn't know its English name.

grounding: A young adult slips into jargon-heavy English with a ward worker and signals status, then notices and includes her.

passage:
Thomas,
You asked what I learnt in placement week. Not what you'd expect.
In the interview I spoke my best English, the careful kind we practised in the hostel corridor. Fine; that's the job. But afterwards the cab driver taking me back to Koramangala asked in Kannada which route I wanted, and I answered in that same polished English, loudly, as if I were still in the interview. He went quiet and drove. At the signal I heard him on the phone, in Kannada: "Big company boy, doesn't speak our language." I do speak it. I grew up speaking it with my Ajji. I had used English to put a wall between us, and he had felt it.
When we reached, I paid and said in Kannada, "Sorry, sir, my head was still in the interview." He laughed and told me about his daughter's engineering exams.
I got the job. I'm keeping the cab ride too.
Vijay

qa.q: Where was the cab taking Vijay after the interview?
qa.a: Back to Koramangala.

qa.q: What might Vijay have felt hearing the driver on the phone?
qa.a: Vijay likely felt a jolt of shame, realising the English had worked as a wall, even though Kannada was his own language.

qa.q: How did Vijay repair the moment, and what could become a habit?
qa.a: He apologised in Kannada and listened to the driver; a habit could be matching the other person's language once the formal setting is over.

qa.q: How did the driver likely see Vijay's loud English?
qa.a: As a status signal from a "big company boy" who would not speak their language, so he went quiet and felt shut out.

grounding: Shows a young adult who uses polished English in an interview and then, without meaning to, as a status wall with a cab driver, and notices it.
